conditional-probability-s1.text: A random sample of 400 adults in a city were asked their main source of news. One of these adults is chosen at random (invented data).

table.caption: Age group and main news source for 400 adults

conditional-probability-s2.title: A screening test
conditional-probability-s2.text: A screening test is used on a large population in which 4% of people have a certain condition. For people with the condition, the test is positive 90% of the time. For people without it, the test is positive 6% of the time. One person from the population is tested.

items.q: What is the probability that the adult gets news mainly online, given that the adult is under 40?

why.correct: Given under 40, the 220 adults under 40 are the new total: $P(\text{online} \mid \text{under } 40) = \frac{132}{220} = 0.6$.
options: That is $\frac{132}{400}$, the joint probability of under 40 and online.
That is $\frac{132}{186}$, the probability of under 40 given online: the condition is reversed.
Right: 132 of the 220 adults under 40.
That is $\frac{186}{400}$, the probability of online for everyone.

items.q: Given that the adult gets news mainly from TV, what is the probability that the adult is under 40?

why.correct: The condition is TV, so divide by the 156 TV viewers: $P(\text{under } 40 \mid \text{TV}) = \frac{66}{156} \approx 0.423$.
options: That is $\frac{66}{220}$, the probability of TV given under 40: the condition is reversed.
That is $\frac{66}{400}$, a joint probability.
That is $\frac{220}{400}$, the probability of under 40 for everyone.
Right: 66 of the 156 TV viewers.

items.q: What is the probability that the adult is 40 or over and gets news mainly from print?

why.correct: This is a joint probability, one cell over all 400: $P(40 \text{ or over} \cap \text{print}) = \frac{36}{400} = 0.09$.
options: Right: 36 of all 400 adults.
That is $\frac{36}{180}$, a conditional probability given 40 or over.
That is $\frac{36}{58}$, a conditional probability given print.
That is $\frac{58}{400}$, the probability of print for everyone.

items.q: What is the probability that the test is positive?

why.correct: Add the two branches that end in positive: $P(\text{positive}) = (0.04)(0.90) + (0.96)(0.06) = 0.036 + 0.0576 = 0.0936$.

mistakes.why: That is only the branch for people with the condition. People without it can test positive too: add (0.96)(0.06).
That adds the two conditional probabilities without weighting them by how many people are on each branch.

items.q: Given that the test is positive, what is the probability that the person has the condition?

mistakes.why: That is P(positive | condition), the reverse. The question gives the positive result and asks about the condition.
That is the joint probability. Divide it by P(positive), 0.0936.

items.q: Which probability is the 0.90 on the tree?

why.correct: The second-stage branches are conditional on the first stage: 0.90 is the chance of a positive test given that the person has the condition.
options: That reverses the condition; it is about 0.385, not 0.90.
P(positive) is 0.0936; it adds two branches.
The joint probability multiplies along the path: 0.036.
Right: on the branch that starts from "condition".
$P(\text{condition} \mid \text{positive})$
$P(\text{positive})$
$P(\text{condition} \cap \text{positive})$
$P(\text{positive} \mid \text{condition})$

items.q: Write an expression for the probability that the person has the condition and tests positive.

mistakes.why: 0.10 is the chance of a negative test for people with the condition. The path to "positive" uses 0.90.
That is the conditional probability alone. Multiply by 0.04, the chance of being on that branch.
0.06 belongs to the people without the condition. Follow the "condition" branch, then "positive".

items.q: The test catches 90% of people with the condition, yet a positive result means only about a 38.5% chance of having it. Why?

why.correct: False positives come from the 96% without the condition: 0.0576 of everyone, more than the 0.036 true positives. So most positive results belong to people without the condition.
options: The test is right 90% of the time for them.
Right: 0.0576 against 0.036.
Paths multiply, and that was done correctly.
It can and does: the two numbers condition on different events.
The test is wrong 90% of the time for people with the condition
Most people do not have it, so false positives outnumber true positives
The tree adds the probabilities along each path instead of multiplying
A 38.5% chance is impossible when the test catches 90% of cases

items.q: Which is the rule for a conditional probability?

why.correct: Given the condition, its outcomes are the new total: divide the joint probability by the probability of the condition, the event after the bar.
options: That divides by the probability of the event before the bar, which gives the reverse conditional probability.
A product is not a conditional probability.
Right: the joint probability over the probability of the condition.
This leaves out the joint event entirely.
$P(A \mid B) = \frac{P(A \cap B)}{P(A)}$
$P(A \mid B) = P(A) \cdot P(B)$
$P(A \mid B) = \frac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)}$
$P(A \mid B) = \frac{P(B)}{P(A)}$

items.q: A bag has 5 red and 3 blue tokens. Two tokens are drawn at random without replacement. What is the probability that both are red?

why.correct: Multiplication rule: $P(\text{1st red}) \cdot P(\text{2nd red} \mid \text{1st red}) = \frac{5}{8} \cdot \frac{4}{7} = \frac{20}{56} \approx 0.357$. After one red is gone, 4 of the 7 tokens left are red.

mistakes.why: That uses $\frac{5}{8}$ twice, as if the first token went back. Without replacement, the second draw is from 7 tokens, 4 of them red.
After one token is drawn, 7 remain, so the second fraction is $\frac{4}{7}$.

items.q: At a store, 40% of customers use a coupon, and 10% of customers both use a coupon and spend more than \$50. Given that a customer uses a coupon, what is the probability that the customer spends more than \$50?

mistakes.why: That is the joint probability. Divide it by P(coupon), 0.40.
That multiplies the two numbers. A conditional probability divides the joint probability by the probability of the condition.

items.q: A report says 80% of drivers injured in crashes were wearing seat belts, and a reader concludes that seat belts are dangerous. What is the flaw?

why.correct: The 80% is P(belt | injured). Most drivers wear belts, so most injured drivers will too. The safety question is P(injured | belt) compared with P(injured | no belt).
options: A large share is expected because most drivers wear belts.
Right: compare P(injured | belt) with P(injured | no belt).
80% is already a share; the problem is which group it is a share of.
A belted driver can be injured, so these events overlap.
There is no flaw: 80% of the injured drivers is a large share
It reverses the condition: the question is the injury rate for belted drivers
The 80% should have been divided by the number of crashes in the report
Seat belts and injuries are mutually exclusive, so 80% is impossible

items.q: In a survey of 300 adults, 120 have a pet, and 45 of the pet owners exercise every day. Write an expression for the probability that a randomly chosen pet owner from the survey exercises every day.

why.correct: Given a pet owner, the 120 pet owners are the total: $P(\text{exercises daily} \mid \text{pet}) = \frac{45}{120} = 0.375$.

mistakes.why: That is the joint probability over all 300 adults. The person is chosen from the 120 pet owners.
That is the probability of owning a pet, not of exercising daily.

items.q: At a school, 60% of students ride the bus. Of the bus riders, 25% are late at least once a month; of the other students, 10% are. What is the probability that a randomly chosen student is late at least once a month?

mistakes.why: That adds the conditional rates without weighting by 0.60 and 0.40, the shares on each branch.
That is only the bus riders who are late. Add the late students who do not ride the bus, (0.40)(0.10).

items.q: At a school, 60% of students ride the bus. Of the bus riders, 25% are late at least once a month; of the other students, 10% are. Given that a student is late at least once a month, what is the probability that the student rides the bus?

mistakes.why: That is P(late | bus), the reverse condition.
That is the joint probability. Divide by P(late), 0.19.

items.q: For the screening test (4% have the condition, 90% positive with it, 6% positive without it), $P(\text{condition} \mid \text{positive}) \approx 0.385$. Build an interpretation in context.

why.correct: The condition, after the bar, names the group: people who test positive. Of them, about 38.5% have the condition.

claim.label: Meaning
options: Of the people who test positive, about 38.5% have the condition
Of the people who have the condition, about 38.5% test positive
About 38.5% of all people tested have the condition and test positive

why.1: That reverses the condition. Of people with the condition, 90% test positive.
why.2: That describes a joint probability, which is 0.036.

evidence.label: So
options: so a positive result alone is far from certain proof of the condition, and a follow-up test makes sense
so the test misses most people who have the condition
so the test is positive for most people

why.1: The test catches 90% of people with the condition.

conclude.model: Of the people in this population who test positive, about 38.5% actually have the condition, so a positive screening result is far from certain and a follow-up test makes sense.
